---
title: "Arc width and continuous reproduction"
---

## Project overview

In the standard continuous reproduction paradigm, participants study a visual feature (e.g., a color) and later reproduce it on a continuous scale (e.g., a color wheel). The angular error between the response and the target is taken as a measure of memory precision — but a single trial's error is just a sample from a distribution, not a direct measure of that trial's memory quality.

In the **uncertainty estimation procedure**, participants additionally draw a symmetric **arc** around their point response, indicating the range of plausible values consistent with their memory. Participants are incentivized to set the arc wisely: points are awarded as

$$
p = (\pi - \alpha) \cdot \mathbf{1}[|y| \le \alpha],
$$

where $y$ is the signed response error and $\alpha$ is the half-width of the arc. Wider arcs are safer (more likely to capture the target) but earn fewer points, creating an **accuracy–confidence tradeoff**.

This website documents analyses, simulations, and model-fitting results.

## Datasets

- **Experiment 1** — 20 participants, manipulating set size (1–8 items) and encoding time / retention interval across two sessions.
- **Honig et al. (2020)** — 12 participants, set size 4, ~1200 trials across four sessions.

## Guide to the notebooks

The sidebar groups notebooks into three sections. Here is the recommended reading order:

### Experiment Description

0. [**Experiment Description & Data Codebook**](notebooks/experiment-description.qmd) — Describes the experimental design of Experiment 1 and provides codebooks for both raw and preprocessed data files.

### Data Exploration

1. [**Exp 1: Exploratory Analysis**](notebooks/exp1-eda.qmd) — Effects of set size, encoding time, and retention interval on point response error and arc width. Fits two-component mixture models and shows that arc width is affected by the same manipulations as response error.
2. [**Exp 1: By-Subject Diagnostics**](notebooks/exp1-by-subject.qmd) — Per-subject distributions of response error and arc width to inspect individual differences and outliers.
3. [**Honig et al.: Data Exploration**](notebooks/honig-explore.qmd) — Preliminary exploration of the Honig et al. dataset.

### Theory & Modeling

4. [**Optimal Arc Width (SDM)**](notebooks/optimal-arc-response.qmd) — Derives the theoretically optimal arc width for any given memory error distribution. Fits the Signal Detection Model (SDM) and shows that empirical arc widths are remarkably close to optimal. *Key notebook.*
5. [**RL Algorithms: Exploration**](notebooks/reinforcement-learning-arc.qmd) — Develops and simulates five reinforcement learning algorithms (algo1–5) for trial-by-trial arc-width adaptation, progressing from simple heuristics to a noisy stochastic-gradient model. *Key notebook.*
6. [**Model Fitting: contraction-expansion (algo4), MLE**](notebooks/fitting-rl-algorithms-algo4-mle.qmd) — Implements maximum-likelihood estimation for the contraction-expansion model (algo4) with logit-scale noise, validates identifiability via 10,000-iteration parameter recovery.
7. [**Model Fitting: noisy-gradient (algo5), MLE**](notebooks/fitting-rl-algorithms-algo5-mle.qmd) — Implements maximum-likelihood estimation for the noisy-gradient model (algo5), validates identifiability via 10,000-iteration parameter recovery.

### Empirical Tests

8. [**Sequential Dependencies**](notebooks/sequential-dependencies.qmd) — Tests whether participants actually adapt arc width after hits/misses, as predicted by the RL models. Controls for regression to the mean via bootstrap shuffling.

## Key concepts

- **[SDM (Signal Discrimination Model)](https://venpopov.github.io/bmm/articles/bmm_sdm_simple.html)** — A model of memory where recall errors follow a distribution parameterized by memory strength $c$ and precision $\kappa$.
- **Arc width** — The confidence interval participants set around their response; $\alpha$ is the half-width in radians.
- **Algorithms 1–5** — A progression of reinforcement learning update rules, from simple multiplicative adjustments to a stochastic gradient ascent model operating on logit-transformed arcs.
